changes.before:
Compare a simply regulated gene, $\dot p=\beta_0-\alpha p$, with an autoregulated gene $\dot p=\beta/(1+(p/K)^n)-\alpha p$ whose parameters are chosen to have the **same steady state** $p_{\rm st}=sK$, so $\beta=\alpha p_{\rm st}(1+s^n)$. Both start from $p=0$ at $t=0$. The simple gene needs $T_{1/2}=\ln2/\alpha$ to reach half of $p_{\rm st}$. The autoregulated gene reaches it faster, and the speed-up factor $\ln 2/(\alpha T_{1/2})$ grows with the repression strength $s$ (the ratio $p_{\rm st}/K$) from $1$ at $s\to0$ toward the limit
$$\ln 2\,(n+1)\,2^{\,n+1}\qquad(s\to\infty),$$
about $5.5$ for $n=1$.
changes.after:

The autoregulated gene reaches it faster, and the speed-up factor $\ln 2/(\alpha T_{1/2})$ grows with the repression strength $s$ (the ratio $p_{\rm st}/K$) from $1$ at $s\to0$ toward the limit
$$\frac{\ln2\,(n+1)}{-\ln(1-2^{-(n+1)})}\qquad(s\to\infty),$$
about $4.82$ for $n=1$.

changes.before:
Time to climb from $0$ to $p_{\rm st}/2$ is $\int_0^{p_{\rm st}/2}dp/\dot p$, computed from the rate law of 2.1. A strong promoter produces at rate $\approx\beta$ while $p<K$, and at matched steady state $\beta=\alpha p_{\rm st}(1+s^n)$ is much larger than the simple gene's $\alpha p_{\rm st}$, so $1/\dot p$ is small along the whole climb. For $s\gg1$ the integrand is $\approx(1+p^n)/\beta$, so $\alpha T_{1/2}\to\bigl[\tfrac s2+\tfrac{(s/2)^{n+1}}{n+1}\bigr]/\bigl[s(1+s^n)\bigr]\to\dfrac{1}{(n+1)2^{n+1}}$, which is the limit above. The theorem is the comparison of this integral with the simple gene's response time of 1.6.

On the interval from zero to half the positive steady state, the net production F(p) is continuous and strictly positive. The integral-as-upper-limit theorem (pma 6.20) therefore gives $T(q)=\int_0^q dp/F(p)$ with derivative $T\prime(q)=1/F(q)$. Along a solution, differentiation yields $dT(p(t))/dt=1$, making this integral the actual first-passage time to q. The full net rate, including removal, is required in the denominator; a production-only approximation needs its own error control.
changes.after:
Keep both production and removal in the inverse-rate time integral. Put $q=p/(sK)$ and $A=s^n$. The normalized half-rise time is
$$\alpha T_{1/2}=\int_0^{1/2}\frac{1+Aq^n}{(1-q)+A(1-q^{n+1})}\,dq.$$
For fixed $0\le q\le1/2$, differentiating this integrand with respect to A has numerator $q^n-1<0$, so the time decreases with repression strength. At A=0 it gives $\ln2$. As A tends to infinity it tends to $q^n/(1-q^{n+1})$, whose integral is $-\ln(1-2^{-(n+1)})/(n+1)$. The denominator stays positive on this compact interval, allowing passage to the limit. Taking $\ln2$ divided by this time gives the stated saturation factor. Dropping removal gives a different approximation and is not the fixed-n strong-repression limit.

The integral-as-upper-limit theorem (pma 6.20) therefore gives $T(q)=\int_0^q dp/F(p)$ with derivative $T\prime(q)=1/F(q)$. Along a solution, differentiation yields $dT(p(t))/dt=1$, making this integral the actual first-passage time to q. The full net rate, including removal, is required in the denominator; a production-only approximation needs its own error control.

changes.before:
A **positively autoregulated** gene is one whose protein activates its own promoter. With a small basal rate $\beta_0$ (without which an empty cell could never start),
$$\frac{dp}{dt}=\beta_0+\beta\,\frac{(p/K)^n}{1+(p/K)^n}-\alpha p .$$
Compare it with a simply regulated gene that has the same steady state $p_{\rm st}$. If the gene has a single, stable steady state, then at every level $p<p_{\rm st}$ the autoregulated gene produces **less** than the simple gene, so it takes longer to rise from zero: its half-rise time exceeds $\ln2/\alpha$, and the rise curve is sigmoidal, with a slow start. If the feedback is strong enough that $\dot p$ vanishes somewhere below $p_{\rm st}$, the gene does not reach $p_{\rm st}$ at all from low levels (see 2.5).
changes.after:
A **positively autoregulated** gene is one whose protein activates its own promoter. With a small basal rate $\beta_0$ (without which an empty cell could never start),
$$\frac{dp}{dt}=\beta_0+\beta\,\frac{(p/K)^n}{1+(p/K)^n}-\alpha p .$$
Compare it with a simply regulated gene that has the same steady state $p_{\rm st}$. If the gene has a single, stable steady state, then at every level $p<p_{\rm st}$ the autoregulated gene produces **less** than the simple gene, so it takes longer to rise from zero: its half-rise time exceeds $\ln2/\alpha$, and the rise starts slowly. A sigmoidal rise can occur when feedback first accelerates and then decelerates the net increase, but weak feedback need not produce an inflection. If the feedback is strong enough that $\dot p$ vanishes somewhere below $p_{\rm st}$, the gene does not reach $p_{\rm st}$ at all from low levels (see 2.5).

changes.before:
At matched steady state the simple gene produces at the constant rate $\alpha p_{\rm st}$, while the activated promoter's rate $\beta_0+\beta h(p)$ is an increasing function of $p$ that only reaches $\alpha p_{\rm st}$ at $p_{\rm st}$. So at each intermediate $p$ the net rate is smaller, and the time $\int dp/\dot p$ is larger. When production depends on $p$ the early rise is slow because there is little activator to amplify (the basal rate must start it), then speeds up as $p$ builds, which gives the sigmoid; the effect is the mirror image of 2.2.

The scalar comparison principle (ode 2.13) formalizes the matched-state comparison. Below the chosen steady state, the increasing production function P(p) is smaller than $P(p_{\rm st})=\alpha p_{\rm st}$, so the simple-gene trajectory is a supersolution for $\dot p=P(p)-\alpha p$. The Hill field is locally Lipschitz on the nonnegative interval, and the trajectories start together; comparison keeps the autoregulated response below the simple response. Reaching the same half-level is therefore slower under the stipulated single-state assumptions; this ordering alone says nothing about the sign of the curve's second derivative.
changes.after:
At matched steady state the simple gene produces at the constant rate $\alpha p_{\rm st}$, while the activated promoter's rate $\beta_0+\beta h(p)$ is an increasing function of $p$ that only reaches $\alpha p_{\rm st}$ at $p_{\rm st}$. So at each intermediate $p$ the net rate is smaller, and the time $\int dp/\dot p$ is larger. When production depends on $p$ the early rise is slow because there is little activator to amplify (the basal rate must start it), it can then speed up if the increased production outweighs the increased removal. For $F(p)=P(p)-\alpha p$ along a rising trajectory, $\ddot p=F\prime(p)F(p)$, so the sign of $F\prime$ decides acceleration. Weak feedback can have $F\prime<0$ throughout the rise and remain concave down, despite being slower than simple regulation.

Below the chosen steady state, the increasing production function P(p) is smaller than $P(p_{\rm st})=\alpha p_{\rm st}$, so the simple-gene trajectory is a supersolution for $\dot p=P(p)-\alpha p$. The Hill field is locally Lipschitz on the nonnegative interval, and the trajectories start together; comparison keeps the autoregulated response below the simple response. Reaching the same half-level is therefore slower under the stipulated single-state assumptions; this ordering alone says nothing about the sign of the curve's second derivative.

changes.before:
In a **negatively autoregulated** gene the protein $p$ is a repressor of its own promoter. With a Hill repression input function (1.3) and first-order removal at rate $\alpha$,
$$\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{\beta}{1+(p/K)^n}-\alpha p .$$
The right side is positive for small $p$ and decreasing, so there is exactly one steady state $p_{\rm st}$, given by $\beta/\bigl(1+(p_{\rm st}/K)^n\bigr)=\alpha p_{\rm st}$, and every trajectory approaches it monotonically. If the promoter is strong ($\beta/\alpha\gg K$) the steady state sits just above the repression threshold, $p_{\rm st}\approx K\,(\beta/\alpha K)^{1/(n+1)}$, far below the level $\beta/\alpha$ that the same promoter would reach without the feedback.
changes.after:
In a **negatively autoregulated** gene the protein $p$ is a repressor of its own promoter. With a Hill repression input function (1.3) and first-order removal at rate $\alpha$,
$$\frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{\beta}{1+(p/K)^n}-\alpha p .$$
The right side is positive for small $p$ and decreasing, so there is exactly one steady state $p_{\rm st}$, given by $\beta/\bigl(1+(p_{\rm st}/K)^n\bigr)=\alpha p_{\rm st}$, and every trajectory approaches it monotonically. If the promoter is strong ($\beta/\alpha\gg K$) at fixed finite $n>0$ the steady state lies above $K$ and grows sublinearly with promoter strength, $p_{\rm st}\approx K\,(\beta/\alpha K)^{1/(n+1)}$, far below the level $\beta/\alpha$ that the same promoter would reach without the feedback.
